>
> **R49-1 in full, because the reasoning is the evidence.**
>
> **The symptom is R48-2's symptom. The cause is R48-2's fix.**
>
> A-68 Part 3 is the right rule and it is stated exactly right: *a bump of a slot's sequence is a
> promise to replace the answer it invalidated.* Part 4 applies it by **removing** a promise the
> transition could not keep — `claimTransition` stops claiming `photoAvailability`, so the nine
> exits that install nothing and answer nothing no longer bump that slot and no longer strand
> anything. That half is correct, and I could not break it: every one of those nine gestures, run
> against a parked read with nothing else in flight, now settles at a terminal state. **`bash
> qa/r49-controls.sh` C1 shows that bare gesture flipping red → green across `d03eac8..HEAD`,
> which is R48-2 genuinely closed.**
>
> Part 5 applies the same rule the other way, by **adding** a promise: a byte write that cannot
> write the availability answer itself sets `availabilityOwed`, and the batch discharges it once
> after its loop. That half is also correct — until you read the guard on the discharge:
>
> ```ts
> if (availabilityOwed && guard.current('doc', g)) await readPhotoAvailability(state.doc);
> ```
>
> The comment above it, in A-68's own words and in the shipped source, is *"Guarded on the ticket
> because a batch that ended on a transition owes nothing: that transition superseded this slot
> itself and issued its own read."* **`guard.current('doc', g)` is false after any bump of the
> `doc` slot**, and Part 4.1's table is a list of nine transitions that bump the `doc` slot and
> then supersede nothing and read nothing. The sentence is true of the six installing reseeds and
> false of precisely the nine exits the ruling one Part earlier was written to fix.
>
> **The trigger is ordinary.** §10.4's halving loop makes `derive` seconds of canvas work per
> file, which A-66 Part 10 item 2 already relies on as *the* likely place for a transition to
> land. So: availability unknown (an establishing read still in flight — §10.6's own `'loading'`),
> a two-file import, file 1 lands and owes, and while file 2 decodes the user taps something that
> claims `doc` and fails or installs nothing. File 2 breaks at the step-4 guard, the fraction
> settles at `0/0`, and the discharge is skipped. Seven producers measured, including a
> `deleteTrip` of a **different** trip, an `openTrip` of a **corrupt** document (§2.9 **A-47**'s
> designed chip-and-banner flow), both `importDoc` refusals, an `adoptTrip` whose `load` rejects,
> and a non-active delete whose cascade rejects. §C5 shows the same thing with **two** overlapping
> batches, where one gesture skips both discharges at once because both hold the same ticket.
>
> **Why this is not a regression, and why that is the finding rather than a defence.** The end
> state was already reachable at `d03eac8` — through R48-2's own mechanism, which A-68 removed.
> C1 measures both: the seven composite gestures are red on **both** sides; the bare gesture is
> red at `d03eac8` and green at HEAD. So A-68 closed the gesture the finding named and left the
> gesture the finding did not name, and **Part 7's invariant claims both**. That is the third
> consecutive ruling in this arc whose enumeration is narrower than its own claim (A-67 Part 7a
> named one line and there were four; A-68 Part 4.1 corrected three exits to nine and Part 5b then
> re-opened seven of them; A-68 Part 9 names three assertions and there are four). The mechanism
> keeps surviving; the **exhaustiveness claims around it** keep not.
>
> **Why MAJOR and not BLOCKER.** Nothing is lost. The bytes are on disk, the records are in the
> document, the batch's fraction settles honestly at `0/0`, no person boundary is crossed, and no
> coordinate or mailbox content is anywhere near this. Closing and re-opening the trip clears it —
> §C4 measures exactly that, three non-installing exits followed by a successful `openTrip`. And
> it is **latent** in the same sense every finding in this arc has been: `grep -rl photosFor
> apps/web/src` is still empty, so nothing renders the spinner today. That is the reason to fix it
> before the surface exists rather than after.
>
> **Why the fix is a ruling and not a line.** At least three shapes are available and they are not
> equivalent. (a) Guard the discharge on the **`photoAvailability`** slot instead — but
> `supersede` returns nothing, so there is no ticket to compare, and adding one changes
> `generation.ts`, which A-68's STATUS forbids. (b) Drop the guard and discharge on `state.doc`
> alone — correct for liveness, but it issues a read for whatever trip the user moved to, whose
> own read is already in flight, so the two now race on the slot that exists to order them (the
> newer claim wins, so it is *safe*, but it spends a port call and contradicts §10.6 property 2's
> *"once per trip open"* in the ordinary case). (c) Make the nine exits answer after all — which
> is A-68 Part 4's own refused option (a), refused because *"a ruling whose correctness depends on
> a builder finding all nine is the ruling that produced this finding."* I have not chosen between
> them and should not.

>
> **The mechanism itself is sound and I could not break it.** `createGenerationGuard` is 10 lines
> of closure state with no dependency, and the four properties A-67 Part 3 claims for it all hold
> under attack: a **four**-transition sequence (A → B → C → A) around a live four-file import stops
> the batch at the first decode that completes on or after the first transition, keeps and
> **persists** everything already dispatched, writes **zero** bytes for every abandoned file, and
> settles `pending`/`total` at `0/0` with `failures: []` — which is R47-1 face 3 (*four picked,
> four written, three lost*) inverted and measured. Three `openTrip`s answered **out of order** all
> resolve to the newest claim on `doc`, `activeTripId` **and** `photos.tripId`. Two browses, a
> browse against `closeBrowse`, and a browse against a trip transition all resolve to the newest
> gesture. `importPhotos` and `importDoc` racing the **same** slot leave neither a record nor a
> byte. And **nine different throwing exits** — a missing id, a corrupt document on `openTrip` and
> on `browseTrip`, garbage and a foreign owner on `importDoc`, a rejecting `storage.delete` on
> both `deleteTrip` branches, a subscriber that throws inside the reseeding `set`, and a
> `createTrip` refused as superseded — every one of them releases: after each, `dispatch` still
> works and an import still lands. There is **no path that leaves a slot claimed forever**, which
> was the failure mode with the widest blast radius available and the first thing I went after.

>
> **R48-2 in full, because the reasoning is the evidence.**
>
> **The symptom is a spinner that never stops. The cause is a guard that is right about ordering
> and silent about completion.**
>
> R46-3 asked *"is this answer for the trip that is open?"* R47-2 showed that question is too
> coarse, A-67 replaced it with *"is this answer the newest one?"*, and that replacement is
> correct: §F's own control — the same slow read with no interloper — reaches `'ready'`, and G4,
> G5 and G6 all hold. What changed is not which answers are **accepted**. It is what happens to
> the ones that are **refused**.
>
> Under R46-3's guard, a refused answer was one whose *trip* had changed, and every path that
> changes the trip installs a new document and issues a new read: `openTrip`, `createTrip`,
> `adoptTrip` and `importDoc` all call `readPhotoAvailability` after their release, and
> `closeTrip` and the active `deleteTrip` reseed to a document-less state where there is no
> listing to strand. The old guard could not strand a listing, because the only thing that could
> trip it was also the thing that replaced it.
>
> A-67 widened the invalidator and did not widen the answerer. `claimTransition()` claims
> `photoAvailability` on **every** transition — Part 5 is explicit that it claims unconditionally,
> *"with no opt-out parameter"* — and three of its exits install nothing:
>
> 1. **`deleteTrip` of a non-active trip.** Part 11 residue 2 discloses the *"deliberate false
>    positive"* here as *"stops an import running for the active one"*. It also stops the active
>    trip's **availability read**, and that consequence is not disclosed anywhere, because it did
>    not exist before this revision.
> 2. **`openTrip` of an id that is not in storage** — `throw new Error('openTrip: no trip … in
>    storage')`, inside the window, by design.
> 3. **`openTrip` of a corrupt document** — `noteOpenFailure(id, err)` then the rethrow, which
>    §2.9 **A-47** deliberately keeps inside the window so the card the user tapped comes back
>    carrying its chip. That path is not an error case bolted on; it is a designed, tested,
>    user-facing flow with a banner and a rescue export, and it now costs the *other* trip its
>    photo listing.
>
> In all three, `state.doc` is unchanged when the dust settles, so the answer that was dropped was
> about the document that is still open — it was *stale by ticket* and *current by subject*. There
> is no second read: `photos.available` stays `null`, `availabilityError` stays `null`, and
> `photosFor` reports `{phase:'loading'}` for as long as the trip stays open. Measured at
> `presentCount: 1` — one read issued, one answer computed, one answer discarded, none re-issued.
>
> **Why that is A-63 and not a new class.** §10.6 property 5 is *"exactly one terminal state
> follows every `'loading'`"*, and A-63 exists because R46-3's finding (`qa/r46-i13b.mjs` §F) was
> literally *"`'loading'` is not transient: two overlapping `openTrip` calls leave it permanently
> — the unresolving spinner A-63 was written to forbid."* This is that sentence with a different
> interloper. The mechanism that closed it for two overlapping opens re-opened it for three other
> gestures, and it did so because the ruling reasoned about **ordering** — which answer wins —
> without reasoning about **liveness** — whether any answer arrives at all. A drop is the right
> disposal for a **losing** read, because a winner is coming behind it. It is the wrong disposal
> for an **orphaned** one, and A-67 does not distinguish them.
>
> **Why MAJOR and not BLOCKER.** Nothing is lost: the bytes are on disk, the records are in the
> document, no person boundary is crossed and no coordinate or mailbox content is anywhere near
> this. The state is wrong, not destroyed, and closing and re-opening the trip clears it. It is
> also **latent** in the same sense every finding in this arc has been — `apps/web` has no photo
> surface yet (`grep -rl photosFor apps/web/src` is empty), so nothing renders the spinner today.
> That is exactly the reason to fix it before the surface exists rather than after: §10.6's
> properties are the contract that surface will be built against, and property 5 is the one that
> says a spinner always stops.
>
> **The fix is a ruling and not a line**, which is why this routes to the architect. Three shapes
> are available and they are not equivalent: (a) re-issue — a dropped read whose subject is still
> `state.doc` re-runs itself, which is closest to *"every branch writes an answer"* but needs a
> bound so two invalidations cannot loop; (b) narrow the claim — a transition that installs no
> document does not take the `photoAvailability` slot, which is Part 5's *"no opt-out parameter"*
> re-opened and which Part 11 residue 2 already names as the answer to its own trigger (*"a fourth
> slot separating 'the document is being replaced' from 'some document is being flushed'"*); or
> (c) give the drop a terminal state — the losing read writes `'unreadable'` with an honest
> message, which is the cheapest and is also the one that lies. I have not chosen between them and
> should not.

> overlapping reads *for the same trip* still let the older one land last. One of its three faces

> read: R47-1's window predates the photo arc entirely (`importPhotos` is merely the first thing in
> this app that dispatches from a promise the user did not just create), and R47-2 is the
> unclosed half of R46-3 — whose own finding text offered *"or carry a generation counter"* as the
> alternative that would have closed both. The repair pass took the narrower option twice, and
> twice the narrower option is exactly right for the case it was routed and exactly not enough for

> **R47-1 in full, because the reasoning is the evidence.**
>
> **The symptom is a lost photograph. The cause is not in the photo path.**
>
> Round 46's R46-1 fix put two guards in `importPhotos`: `isLiveTrip(tripId)` before the `write`,
> and `state.doc?.id !== tripId` before the `dispatch`. Both are correct, and §B of this round's
> probe could not fool either of them — not with a third trip, not with a return trip. What the
> second guard cannot know is that **passing it is not the same as the record surviving.**
>
> `openTrip` is:
>
> ```ts
> if (!(await flushForTransition())) return state;          // :1261 — rule 6a, the flush
> const stored = await ports.storage.load(id);              // :1262 — a real IndexedDB read
> …
> set({ ...initialState(), …, doc }, { reseed: true });     // :1277 — state.doc moves
> ```
>
> §4.2 rule 6a is *"a pending write is never outlived by its document"*, and `flushForTransition`'s
> own body already knows why that is hard: QA **R5-1** established that *"a flush is not a moment —
> it is an `await` long enough for the user to type into"*, which is why its loop re-asserts
> `dirty()` **after every write** rather than sampling it once. **That insight stops at the loop's
> closing brace.** `ports.storage.load(id)` is another await, on the far side of it, and nothing
> re-asserts `dirty()` across it. Anything dispatched there lands in a document that `set` is about
> to replace; the `scheduleSave()` it armed fires against `forTripId = A` when `state.doc` is `B`,
> and `attemptSave`'s *"a late timer is dropped, never retargeted"* — which is right, and is R3-2's
> own fix — drops it. The edit is gone and `persistence.status` is `'idle'`.
>
> **Face 1 is that statement with no photographs in it**, and it is how I found the cause rather
> than the symptom: park `openTrip`'s `storage.load`, `dispatch({type:'setTripMeta', …})` inside
> the window, let the transition finish. In memory the title is `"EDITED IN THE WINDOW"`; in
> storage it is `"A"`; the indicator says `'idle'`. `qa/r4-switch.mjs` §9's standing assertion is
> *"no tab renders 'Saved' over a document storage does not hold"* — this is that, on a sequence
> that probe does not drive. **It is latent rather than live**: `openTrip` is only reached from the
> Library, the Map tab and the Profile tab, and none of them has an editable field mounted, so
> today nothing in `apps/web` can dispatch a *typed* edit into that window.
>
> **Face 2 is the producer that can.** `importPhotos` is the only thing in this application that
> dispatches from a promise the user did not just create, and §10.4's halving loop makes `derive`
> *deliberately* seconds of canvas work per file. A decode resolving inside `storage.load` passes
> the `:1541` guard honestly — `state.doc.id` really is still `tripId` at that instant — writes the
> record into a document the next line discards, and the batch then breaks on the following file
> with its bytes already written. **Two stranded derivative pairs, against A-66 Part 7's *"exactly
> one derivative pair per abandoned batch"*.**
>
> **Face 3 is why this is MAJOR and not a bound that is off by one.** The batch only ends when the
> dispatch guard *fails*, and re-opening the **same** trip never fails it — `state.doc?.id ===
> tripId` on both sides of the transition. So the loop runs on, and every re-open whose
> `storage.load` swallows a decode costs one more photograph. Measured, with the store's own
> `defaultScheduler` and its real debounce (which is what `apps/web` runs on — `apps/web/src/store.ts`
> passes no scheduler port): **four files picked, four decoded, four written, three lost, one kept,
> `failures: []`, `pending: 0`.** The user never left trip A. They tapped it again — from the Map or
> the Profile tab, which is exactly where `App.tsx:79` and `:93` call `openTrip` — while their
> photographs were still importing, which is the single most natural thing to do when you are
> waiting for photographs to import.
>
> **Why that is not covered by A-66.** A-66 Part 5 item 3 is the sentence that makes the silent
> drop honest: *"the outcome is self-evident and the remedy is the affordance they just used. The
> user returns to trip A and sees fewer photographs than they picked."* Every clause of that rests
> on the user having **navigated away** — Part 5 item 1's cancel precedent, Part 4's
> session-versus-file distinction, Part 3's observation that the transition is what reset the
> report. Here they did not navigate away, nothing was abandoned, and the store's own guard said
> the photograph had been added. And A-66's *"the trigger that reopens this ruling"* is **a
> producer of abandoned files that is not a user navigation** — which is precisely what this is,
> one layer down. I am not asking for the sixth arm: Part 3's misattribution argument is untouched
> and I agree with it. I am reporting that the ruling's factual premise — *"exactly one file has
> written derivatives with no record"* — is false, and that the leak it makes acceptable is
> unbounded.
>
> **Why MAJOR and not BLOCKER.** The originals are untouched in the user's own library (A-57 Part 9
> residue 1), so the recovery is a re-pick; nothing crosses a person boundary; no other trip's data
> is reached. That is the same reckoning rounds 45 and 46 applied to R45-3 and R46-1, both
> *"unreachable and unreportable"* and both MAJOR.
>
> **The fix, and it is small.** `openTrip`, `adoptTrip` and `importDoc` each need `dirty()`
> re-asserted across the awaits that follow their flush — either by moving `flushForTransition()`
> to just before the `set`, or by re-running it if the document moved. The store already owns the
> idiom twice: `flushForTransition`'s own R5-1 loop, and `doMerge`'s `if (state.doc !== doc)` check
> *inside* its `chainOntoSaving` link, which exists for exactly this reason one subsystem over and
> whose comment says so (*"checking before `chainOntoSaving` is a check-then-act with an
> interleaving point in the middle"*). The photo half needs nothing beyond that.
>
> **The one line for the architect**, and it is a sentence rather than a mechanism: **A-66 Part 7's
> bound is stated as a fact about the loop and read as a fact about the system.** It is right about
> the loop. Once R47-1 is fixed the two coincide again — but the sentence *"bounded at one
> derivative pair per abandoned batch, swept by `removeTrip`"* is doing real load-bearing work in
> A-66 Part 7 and in A-62 Part 8 residue 2's trigger, and a reader should know it is a property of
> one function's control flow and not an invariant anything enforces.

>
> **The send-back is not about the key. It is about the three places a photo write crosses a trip
> boundary that the key cannot police, and one of them is a regression this pass introduced.**
> `importPhotos` captures the owning `TripId` before its first `await` — a line A-62 is the reason
> for — and then dispatches the document record against whatever trip is open when the decode
> finishes. Switch trips while a batch is decoding and the bytes land under trip A while the
> record lands in trip B. At `9635207` that was a misfiling you could still look at, because the
> byte key was a bare `PhotoId`; at `70b9ee6` the photograph is gone, reported `'ready'` in the
> session that lost it and `'missing'` after a re-open, with the derivative stranded under a key
> nothing will ever name. **A-62 turned a benign bug into a lost photograph, and that is exactly
> the kind of thing a confirmation round exists to catch.**

> **R46-1 in full, because the reasoning is the evidence.**
>
> A-62 put tenancy in the byte key, and `importPhotos` was changed in the same pass to match. Its
> new line is `:1415`, with a comment that states the rule exactly:
>
> > *"Captured before the first `await`: every byte written by this batch belongs to the trip the
> > user was looking at when they picked the files, and §10.3's key now says so. A `state.doc.id`
> > read after an await could name a different trip (§4.2 rule 6's shape, one subsystem over) and
> > would file the bytes under a tenancy that never asked for them."*
>
> That is right, and it is half of the invariant. The loop has three `await`s —
> `pickImages`, `derive` and `write` — and then, at `:1461`, `this.dispatch({ type: 'addPhoto' })`,
> which writes into `state.doc`, which is **live**. So the byte side is pinned to the trip the user
> picked from and the record side is pinned to whatever trip is open when the decode finishes.
> Nothing checks that they are the same trip.
>
> `pickImages` is a modal `<input type=file>` and the app is not interactive while it is up.
> **`derive` is not.** It is `createImageBitmap` plus two canvas passes per file, over a batch, and
> §10.4's halving loop makes it deliberately more work rather than less. During those seconds the
> library, the brand button and every other trip in the app are live. Three faces, all measured in
> `qa/r46-i13b.mjs` §D with nothing injected but a 60 ms `derive`:
>
> 1. **Open trip A, import, tap "back to all trips", open trip B.** The record lands in **B**; the
>    bytes are keyed `[A, photo-1]`. B's listing reads **`ready`** for the rest of the session —
>    because the optimistic update at `:1487` correctly checks `state.photos.tripId === state.doc.id`,
>    and by then both are B — while `read(B, 'photo-1', 'thumb')` returns `null`. §10.6 property 3's
>    whole point is *"a surface never renders a `null` object URL"*, and this is a listing that tells
>    it to. After a re-open the same photo reads **`missing`**, which is §10.6 property 3's
>    *"this photo's image is no longer stored on this device"* over bytes that are on this device.
>    `orphanPhotoBytes` reports nothing, so the stranded derivative is unreachable **and**
>    unreportable — R45-3's exact words, on a new path.
> 2. **The same with `{kind:'day', dayId}`.** The attach ref is captured with the call and the day
>    belongs to trip A, so the record lands in trip B pointing at a day trip B does not have.
>    `validateTrip` reports **`photo_attach_dangling`**: the store has written a document its own
>    validator calls invalid.
> 3. **Delete the trip mid-decode.** `deleteTrip`'s cascade runs, then `write(tripId, …)` lands
>    **after** it. Measured: `[trip-1, photo-1]` sitting in both byte stores with no document, no
>    library row and no orphan report — §6.3's *"no row and no blob without a live tenancy
>    reference"* broken by a race rather than by a missing cascade. The user is told
>    `storage_failed`, which is untrue: storage worked, the trip went away. (`closeTrip` mid-decode
>    is the same shape with the same wrong reason.)
>
> **Why this is a regression and not just an old bug.** I ran the identical sequence in a
> `git worktree` at `9635207`. There the byte key was a bare `PhotoId`, so the record in trip B
> found its bytes: the listing read `ready`, `read('photo-1', 'thumb')` returned the derivative, and
> the user saw their photograph — in the wrong trip, which is a real but survivable bug. At
> `70b9ee6` the same tap sequence loses the photograph. **A-62 is the right ruling and this is the
> cost of implementing half of it**: putting tenancy in the key made every mismatch between "which
> trip owns the bytes" and "which trip owns the record" fatal instead of cosmetic, and the only
> place that mismatch can be created is the one function that writes both.
>
> **Why MAJOR and not BLOCKER.** The original photograph is untouched on the user's device, so
> nothing is unrecoverable; the stranded derivative is swept whenever trip A is deleted; there is no
> leak and no other person's data. That is the same reckoning round 45 applied to R45-3, which was
> also *"unreachable and unreportable"* and was also MAJOR. It is nonetheless the worst thing in
> this arc and it is new.
>
> **The fix is a re-check, not a redesign.** `importPhotos` already knows the answer: it holds
> `tripId`. One guard before the dispatch — *if the active document is no longer `tripId`, stop the
> batch, remove the bytes it just wrote, and report a named failure that is not `storage_failed`* —
> closes all three faces, and is the same shape as `flushForTransition`'s rule 6b and as `doMerge`'s
> own `if (state.doc !== doc)` check at `:836`, which exists for exactly this reason one subsystem
> over. The store already has the idiom; the photo path did not get it.

> **R45-1 in full, because the reasoning is the evidence.**
>
> A-57 Part 5 took `SCHEMA_VERSION` to 2 with an argument I agree with. `migrate.ts`'s own docstring
> is the rule: *"a field that is additive with a total default does not earn a `schemaVersion` bump
> … a bump is reserved for a value widening that an older client would silently drop."* `photos`
> **is** records; an old build opening a v2 document and saving it deletes the user's photo
> attachments and orphans megabytes it cannot see. So the version moves and *"an older build
> refuses the document loudly — which is the correct outcome."*
>
> That reasoning is about the **old** build reading a **new** document. It says nothing about the
> new build reading an old one, and that direction is what `migrateDoc` exists for. The builder
> wrote it, correctly: `fromJSON(migrateDoc(v1))` produces a valid `Trip` with `photos: []`, and I
> verified that at `497c116`. `packages/core/test/photos.test.ts:208` asserts it. `test/stats-storage.test.ts:1700`
> drives a v1 fixture through it. `qa/i7a-idb-rowkeys.mjs` phase 3 proves the *port* hands a v1
> document back byte for byte, and says in its own assertion label that migrating it is *"core's
> job and not the port's."*
>
> **Core's job is never invoked.** I walked every `.ts` and `.tsx` file under `packages/core/src`,
> `packages/client/src` and `apps/web/src` for a call to `migrateDoc` and found **zero**. Every
> reference in the repository is a test, a QA probe, `index.ts`'s re-export, or a comment. The five
> production `core.fromJSON` call sites in `store.ts` — `openTrip` (`:1208`), `browseTrip`
> (`:1246`), `importDoc` (`:1603`), the summary rescan (`:913`) and the two-tab merge (`:794`) —
> all hand the raw stored string straight to the parser, and `fromJSON:481` refuses anything whose
> `schemaVersion !== SCHEMA_VERSION`.
>
> `migrate.ts`'s pre-I-13 docstring said the call site *"exists now so that the call site is in
> place before the first real migration, rather than being retrofitted into every reader."* It was
> not in place. It was never in place — the whole mechanism was dormant while there was only one
> version, and I-13 is the commit that turned a dormant defect into a live one.
>
> **The blast radius, measured rather than reasoned about.** Against a document minted by a build
> at `598cd7f` and aged exactly as a v1 build wrote it (no `photos` key, `schemaVersion: 1`):
>
> - `core.fromJSON` → `TripParseError: unsupported schemaVersion 1 — this build reads version 2`.
> - `store.openTrip` → the same error, recorded in `openFailures` and rethrown. The trip is
>   **not openable**.
> - `store.importDoc` → the same error. **Every backup file the user has ever exported is
>   unrestorable**, including the rescue export I-8e §C ships for exactly this situation.
> - The summary rescan (`:913`) catches it into `rescan.unreadable`, so **every** pre-existing trip
>   is marked *"could not be read"* on the next library refresh.
> - `refreshLibrary` still lists the trips, because summary rows are `SUMMARY_VERSION` 5 and did
>   not move. So the user sees their whole travel history and can open none of it.
>
> **And the rendered face, in the real built app.** `qa/r3-upcast.mjs` is a standing probe from
> round 3 that plants a genuine `schemaVersion: 1` document (`qa/r3-upcast.mjs:42`) into a real
> IndexedDB and boots the production bundle over it. At `497c116` it prints
> *"1 trip is not up to date yet. One trip's file could not be read, so its details are the last
> ones"* and then times out at §3 waiting for *"Add a stop"*, because the trip will not open. **That
> probe is not in I-13's BUILD-NOTES list of what was run**, and it would have caught this in one
> command.
>
> The message the user gets is the one written for a document from the **future** — *"this build
> reads version 2"*, whose companion sentence is *"Update the app."* There is no app to update to.
>
> **The fix is small and its shape is a ruling, not a patch.** `migrateDoc` in front of `fromJSON`
> at all five call sites is the obvious answer and is probably wrong as written — `browseTrip` and
> the merge read documents for comparison, and a migration that silently rewrites one of them is
> a different decision from a migration that runs on open. The narrow correct version is almost
> certainly *inside* `fromJSON`, which is where every reader already goes and where §2.10 already
> exposes one entry point; that also makes the refusal message for a **newer** document
> (`migrateDoc`'s own *"Update the app."*) the one users actually see, which is what A-57 Part 5
> intended. Either way, whatever lands needs a test that opens a document written by the
> **previous release** rather than one hand-built at the current version — the property no test in
> this repository currently has, which is why 1,316 of them are green over a build nobody's
> existing data can open.
>
> **R45-2 in full, for the same reason.**
>
> §10.3 keys `photos` and `photoThumbs` by bare `PhotoId`. §6.2 rule 1 — which §10.5 point 3 cites
> approvingly for the Phase 3 case — says the opposite: *"an object key is
> `trip/{tripId}/photo/{photoId}`, so a blob's owner is recoverable from its key alone."* §10.3's
> departure is not arbitrary: it is what makes `read`/`write`/`remove`/`present` simple and what
> lets `present(ids)` be one `getAllKeys()` call. The cost is that tenancy is recoverable only by
> parsing a document, which is exactly what `indexedDbStorage.delete`'s `photoIdsOf` does.
>
> That works as long as a `PhotoId` belongs to one trip. `importDoc` breaks the assumption, and it
> breaks it on the path the brief calls *"backup/restore of the user's own exports."* Its
> id-collision branch is careful — *"the injected `IdFactory` is deterministic … so a fresh id can
> itself collide with a stored one. Keep minting until it does not"* — and it mints exactly one
> id: the trip's. The photo records inside the document keep theirs. So after restoring a backup of
> a trip you still have, `trip-1` and `trip-2` both reference `photo-1`, `photo-2`, `photo-3`, and
> the byte store holds one copy of each.
>
> Three shipped operations then destroy data across the trip boundary, all measured in
> `qa/r45-i13.mjs` §C:
>
> 1. **`deleteTrip` on the restored copy.** The store's cascade removes the ids in `state.doc.photos`
>    (`:1324`); `apps/web`'s cascade removes the ids in the stored document (`storage.ts`'s
>    `photoIdsOf`). Both name the shared ids. Measured: the original trip goes from 3 photographs
>    to `missing: 3 of 3`.
> 2. **`removePhoto` in either trip.** Measured: `missing: 1`, in the trip the user never touched.
> 3. **`reclaimPhotoBytes`.** Its guard is *"it refuses any id that a live asset still references,
>    rather than trusting the caller's list"* — and `live` is `state.doc?.photos`, the **active**
>    trip only. An orphan recorded while trip B was open can be reclaimed while trip A still
>    references it. (Not separately reproduced: reaching it needs a failed byte delete first, and
>    the two paths above are sufficient and simpler.)
>
> None of this needs a second person, a server, or a hostile input. It needs the user to restore
> their own backup — the one operation `importDoc` exists for — and then delete the copy.
>
> **Why this is the architect's before it is the builder's.** The one-line builder fix is to
> re-mint photo ids in `importDoc` alongside the trip id, and it should probably land regardless.
> But it is a patch on one path, and the invariant it restores — *a `PhotoId` names bytes belonging
> to exactly one trip* — is stated nowhere in §10, is not checked by `validateTrip` (R45-15), and
> is silently assumed by three separate call sites. §6.2 rule 1 already names the key shape that
> makes it structural, and §10.3's reasons for departing from it (one `getAllKeys()`, a simple
> port) are worth re-examining now that the cost has a measurement rather than a hypothesis. That
> is a §10.3 amendment, not a `store.ts` edit.

> placed an obligation beside `travelStats`' grandfathered throw — the surfaces must *"show a
> refusal … rather than a blank screen or an unhandled rejection"* — and `travelHistory` is
> where that obligation is discharged, once, for both `Profile.tsx` and `WorldMap.tsx`. The new
> code puts a **partial** function inside it.
>
> `rowStatsReadable` does `for (const c of row.cities)` with no guard. Three row shapes make
> that throw, and one makes it lie:
>
> - **`cities` absent.** This is not hypothetical and it is not hand-edited storage. It is the
>   **version-1 summary row**, exactly as `SUMMARY_VERSION`'s own docstring ledger defines it:
>   *"**1** — the Phase 1 / Phase 2a row: `{id, title, startDate, endDate, datePrecision,
>   cityCount, dayCount, stopCount, poolCount, revision}`"*. `cities` arrives at version **2**.
>   `qa/i7a-idb-rowkeys.mjs`'s `ROW_GEN1` fixture is that shape, and `qa/r3-upcast.mjs` seeds
>   *"a genuine **version-1** `cairn` database … the shape Jacob's browser actually holds"*.
> - **`cities: null`** and **`cities: [null]`** — the hand-edited-storage population A-59 Part 5
>   names as this feature's whole reason for existing.
> - **`cities: 'nope'`** — a string is iterable, so the loop runs over characters, `c.firstDay`
>   is `undefined` on each, and the row comes back **`true`: readable**. Same missing guard,
>   opposite symptom, and the wrong answer rather than a loud one.
>
> I drove the first case end to end through the **shipped store**, not through a hand-built
> state: seed a version-1 row and a version-5 row through `saveIfVersion`, `refreshLibrary()`,
> then read. `summaryScan(state).phase` is `'stale'` — this is the window `refreshLibrary`
> legitimately leaves open, which `travelStats`' own R28-3 comment describes and which round 43
> §L already measured for version-4 rows. In that window:
>
> - `rowLifecycle(v1, today)` → `'completed'` and `rowDatesReadable(v1)` → `true`. **The three
>   older row gates are all total over it.** Only the new one is not.
> - `travelHistory(state, today)` at **`7ef18c9`** → `{ok: false, message: 'row.cities is not
>   iterable', rowId: null}`. Degraded, contained, and the designed refusal renders.
> - `travelHistory(state, today)` at **`b574dc5`** → **throws** `TypeError: row.cities is not
>   iterable`, out of the catch.
>
> The `travelStats` throw itself is pre-existing and out of I-12a's scope; what I-12a changed is
> that the boundary no longer holds it. Downstream, `App.tsx`'s per-tab `TabBoundary` catches
> the render throw, so the user gets *"The Profile tab could not be shown"* plus a `console.error`

> the Map tab fails the same way. That containment is why this is MAJOR and not a BLOCKER; it is
> also read from `App.tsx` rather than measured in a browser, since I-12a opens no `.tsx` file.

> **The fix is one line and it is free.** I injected `for (const c of row.cities ?? [])` and ran
> the **full suite: 1235 pass / 0 fail** — nothing pins the throw, so nothing has to be
> renegotiated. One judgement belongs to the builder, and it is worth stating rather than

> | **The four things the builder said it could not verify, and what I found** | **(1) The four-pane layout was never looked at in a browser.** I looked, at **four** viewports (390 × 820, 360 × 640, 1440 × 700, 1100 × 900): all four panes render, none collapses, none overlaps, the detached pane is last, is captioned *"DISTANT PARTS OF FR US"* (never *"Shown separately"*), its `aria-label` names both codes, both codes are drawn twice with identical attribution, one chip each, no React key warning, every chip drills down. It is also where R38-3's worst number lives — `inset-2` at **21.3%** of its cell. **(2) Is `i8h-render.mjs` §A's `--pane-aspect` shortcut sound?** **Yes**, and it is sound for a stronger reason than sampling: A-50's rule cannot letterbox *algebraically*. With `width: min(100%, cap × aspect)`, `aspect-ratio: aspect`, `max-height: cap` — if `cap × aspect < W` then width is `cap × aspect` and height is exactly `cap`, at the clamp and not past it; if `cap × aspect ≥ W` then width is `W` and height is `W / aspect ≤ cap`. Either way the box has the pane's own aspect and `max-height` never fires. The shortcut varies the only free input. Its one gap is that it plants every pane's aspect on the **main** pane's element, so an inset's or detached pane's box (45% flex basis, 170 px cap) is only covered by §B's six libraries — which is why I re-ran it as **92 real page loads including insets and detached panes at four viewports**, and it holds. **(3) `countryParts`' cost was not profiled.** Measured on one run against `09f7ce4` in a worktree: `worldMapFrame` at the 239-code ceiling is **31.0 ms** at `dea2c67` against **37.7 ms** at `09f7ce4`; at a realistic 25 codes, **1.2 ms**. `countryParts` over all 239 codes is **1.95 ms**. The new call is not the cost driver and I-8h is not slower. **(4) Nothing was measured on a real phone.** Still true — I have no device either. Against the true centre of France (46.5°N, 2.5°E) those same pairs are FR–DE 780 km, FR–GR 1,929, FR–FI 2,500, FR–MA 2,232 — i.e. every one of them is on the other side of the threshold, and the ordering of "near" and "far" is **inverted**: France is closer to Morocco than to Germany only because of French Guiana. Driven end to end (`qa/r36-atlas.mjs` §B4): a library of **two trips to France and one to Greece** produces `main[FR] w2 · inset-1[GR] w1` — a **main pane 64.1° wide for one country**, four fifths of it Atlantic Ocean, with the country that is actually 1,900 km from France exiled to the *"Shown separately"* inset. The rulings that would have to move are C2, and residue 1′'s reopen trigger, which as written says *"not before"* a library contains one of five codes that a French traveller will never have. **Why MAJOR and not BLOCKER:** nothing is lost, mis-attributed or destroyed — I1/I2 hold on every fixture (§E), France is still drawn, still counted, still tappable, still carries its `tripIds` — the map is merely of the wrong subject, which is precisely the severity the manager assigned this class of defect at R33-1. **Repro:** `node qa/r36-atlas.mjs` §A and §B4. |
> | **R36-2 — the alphabet decides the panes, and A-41 constraint 2 says it does not** | A-41 constraint 2, one of Jacob's four: *"No special case for any country, region or destination type. Nothing here reads which country a code is. **Clustering is a function of coordinates**; ranking is a function of the traveller's own record."* C3 then specifies the partition as *"a point joins the **first** group containing a member within the threshold"* — first-fit, not the transitive closure — and `clusterPoints` implements exactly that (asserted directly in `qa/r36-atlas.mjs` §B1: the hand case `[0°, 80°, 40°]` at 5,000 km gives `[[0,2],[1]]`, and over the whole 239-code index first-fit gives **9** groups where a union-find single-linkage gives **1**). First-fit is not transitive, so **the input order is part of the answer**, and the input order is `travelStats`' canonical **ascending ISO code**. That makes the alphabet a second input to the clustering, which is what constraint 2 forbids in the sentence it forbids continent tables in. **It is not theoretical and it is not rare.** Over a 69-code set of well-travelled countries there are **122** three-country libraries in which two countries **less than 1,600 km apart** land in different clusters, and the tightest is `{FR, HU, SI}` where **Hungary and Slovenia — 350 km apart — are separated**. The cleanest one to look at, driven end to end (§B2): `{AE 1 trip, AT 1 trip, GR 3 trips}` → **`main[AE,GR] w4 · inset-1[AT] w1`**. Austria, **1,326 km** from Greece, is the outlier; the United Arab Emirates, **3,281 km** from Greece, shares the main pane with it. The mechanism is exactly first-fit: `AE` opens group 1, `AT` is 4,422 km from `AE` so it opens group 2, and `GR` then tests **group 1 first**, is within 4,000 km of `AE`, and joins it — never reaching group 2, which it is three times closer to. **The proof that this is order and not geometry:** hand `worldMapFrame` the identical three rows as `AT, GR, AE` and it returns **one pane** containing all three. The product never does that, because rows arrive sorted — so the shipped path always takes the worse branch of the two. **Why architect and not builder:** C3 names first-fit in as many words, calls it *"the identical rule `clusterStops` has used since Phase 1"*, and A-41 Part 6 makes a single kernel a hard requirement; changing it to a transitive closure changes `clusterStops` and `focusCluster` and therefore the day map, which is a core-invariant decision and explicitly not a builder's. **Why MAJOR:** the visible outcome is a *"Shown separately"* caption naming the wrong country — the surface actively asserts that Austria is the distant one — and it is reachable from a three-country library. **Why not BLOCKER:** nothing is lost or mis-attributed; §E's I1/I2 accounting holds on every fixture including this one. **Repro:** `node qa/r36-atlas.mjs` §B1 and §B2. |

On top of that the surface **makes a claim the geometry does not support**: `WorldMap.tsx:143` prints *"Zoomed out to a readable minimum"* for the 1.20 km frame and prints nothing for the 1.76 km one. **This is an architect call, not a builder one**, because A-40 clause 2 states as a ruling that *"the min-span guard … is how 'a one-country history must not open at a rooftop zoom' is satisfied — by the guard that already exists, not by a second one"*, and that sentence is false at world-map scale. > | **R28-1 — the BLOCKER, in full, because the reasoning is the evidence** | `derive/summary.ts:23` is `dayNumber(d) = Math.floor(Date.UTC(y, m-1, dd)/86400000)`. **`Date.UTC` applies the ES legacy two-digit-year rule**: a `year` argument of 0–99 means 1900–1999. So `dayNumber('0001-01-01') === dayNumber('1901-01-01')` — measured, both `-25202`. And `derive/summary.ts:28-30` stringifies `getUTCFullYear()` with `padStart(2,'0')` on the *month and day* but **no padding on the year**, so a genuine year below 1000 comes back three digits: `fromDayNumber(dayNumber('0500-06-01'))` is `"500-06-01"`, which `parseIsoDate` — in the same file, eight lines up — throws on. Three consequences, each run: (1) **`travelStats` emits a date its own parser rejects.** A row starting `0500-06-01` reports `firstVisit: "500-06-01"`. (2) **Two trips 1900 years apart are one interval.** A year-`0001` trip and a year-`1901` trip over the same days report `daysTravelled: 10`, not 20 — the union collapsed them. (3) **The product-reachable one.** `apps/web/src/views/PastTripForm.tsx:76` gates the Year field on `/^\d{4}$/` and nothing else, and the input at `:208` strips non-digits and truncates to four — so `0202`, a plausible mistype of `2020`, is typeable and valid. The trip is in storage, is the only copy, and can never be opened again — `Library.tsx` badges it *"could not be read"*, which is graceful degradation around **data that is gone**. ### R31-1 — the reproduction

All three commands run from `cairn/`, each in a throwaway `git worktree add --detach` at `4e7b31d`
that is removed afterwards. Written as heredocs rather than committed under `qa/` because this
round was instructed to write no file but this one.

```bash
# 1. H4 — "while we are in here, bring STALE summary rows current."
#    One edit in ensureReady(), in class with G12/G13. Plus the honest maintenance step a
#    builder shipping this would take: re-derive the two vacuity-control anchors that the
#    transaction-scope line drifts, exactly as their own message instructs.
python3 - "$WT/cairn" <<'PY'
import sys
root = sys.argv[1]
p = root + "/apps/web/src/ports/storage.ts"
s = open(p).read()
old = "          const tx = db.transaction([DOCS, VERSIONS], 'readwrite');\n          const versions = tx.objectStore(VERSIONS);"
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, "          const tx = db.transaction([DOCS, SUMMARIES, VERSIONS], 'readwrite');\n          const versions = tx.objectStore(VERSIONS);\n          const sums = tx.objectStore(SUMMARIES);", 1)
loop = "              for (const key of docKeys.result) {\n                if (have.has(String(key))) continue;"
assert loop in s
s = s.replace(loop, """              const stale = sums.getAll() as IDBRequest<TripSummaryRow[]>;
              stale.onsuccess = () => {
                for (const r of stale.result) {
                  if (r.summaryVersion >= CURRENT_SUMMARY) continue;
                  sums.put({ ...r, countriesVisited: r.countryCodes.length, daysTravelled: r.dayCount }, r.id);
                }
              };
""" + loop, 1)
s = s.replace("const DEAD_META = 'meta';", "const DEAD_META = 'meta';\nconst CURRENT_SUMMARY = 4;", 1)
open(p, "w").write(s)
# re-derive the drifted anchors (both G12's and G13's first anchor is the tx-scope line)
t = root + "/test/stats-storage.test.ts"
ts = open(t).read()
a = "      \"          const tx = db.transaction([DOCS, VERSIONS], 'readwrite');\\n          const versions = tx.objectStore(VERSIONS);\","
assert ts.count(a) == 2
ts = ts.replace(a, "      \"          const tx = db.transaction([DOCS, SUMMARIES, VERSIONS], 'readwrite');\\n          const versions = tx.objectStore(VERSIONS);\\n          const sums = tx.objectStore(SUMMARIES);\",")
open(t, "w").write(ts)
PY

# 2. Measure. Per arm, then whole-file, then typecheck.
for pat in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  node --test --test-reporter=tap --test-name-pattern="6b-1b-$pat: STARTING STATE" \
    test/stats-storage.test.ts | grep -E '^# (tests|pass|fail)'
done
node --test --test-reporter=tap test/stats-storage.test.ts | grep -E '^# (tests|pass|fail)'
npm run typecheck
```

**Measured:** arms 1–5 **all GREEN**; whole file **28 pass / 0 fail**; `typecheck` clean on both

neither the `: number` sweep nor the numeric-literal sweep at `test/stats-storage.test.ts:1258`

`PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers node --experimental-strip-types <scratch> --fault=h4`

full account. Three things make it worth a MAJOR rather than a note. **(1) It reaches persisted

transaction that bypasses the port, 14 keys before the second open and 16 after, with

clause 2 and A-31 Part 6 exist to forbid. **(2) It is caught by nothing, including the out-of-band
check, and what separates caught from uncaught is the SPELLING.** Exit criterion 6 is 18/0. The
name-based tripwire cannot see it (the value is an expression, not a `: number` and not a numeric
literal). 6b-1b cannot see it (the upcast is empty in every one of its four arms). 6b-4 cannot see

because *"a static check over an argument expression cannot see what happened to the binding
before the call"* — turns out to be the **only** thing that can, and only for one of the two ways
to write it. **Measured, both:** spell the upcast write `tx.objectStore(SUMMARIES).put({ ...r, … },
r.id)` and 6b-2's pinned site count goes red at three sites (`qa/r30-exit6c.sh` **G12b**, RED 1);
hoist the store to `const sums = tx.objectStore(SUMMARIES)` — which is what anyone writes when the
same store is touched twice in one transaction, and this transaction already hoists `versions` for
exactly that reason — and the literal text `objectStore(SUMMARIES).put` still appears twice, so
**G12 is green**. The gate's residual coverage of this path is a regex over a call-chain spelling.

over a seeded recorder — three lines, and it closes G12 permanently — or A-36 Part 2's sentence
narrows from *"every value that reaches its summary store"* to *"every value written by a mutating
interface method"* and the upcast joins Part 6 as a residue with a trigger. Which one is right is
the architect's call because it changes what the gate claims about itself, and this project has
now spent three rounds on exactly that question. **What R30-1 is not:** it is not a defect in
shipped code (the port is clean in Node and in Chromium, across a second open — I ran the control),
and it is not a §0.5 failure of A-36's own bug, which 6b-1b catches four ways.

anchors including a low-era one, 3,652 and 3,654 in both directions, the widened span with a

two forms' catch paths read rather than assumed. A-36: G7, G7b (`Object.assign(summary, …)`), G8,
G11 (a key **dropped** on read), the double's four outcome assertions, the vacuity control's own
anchor guard, and 6b-4 in real Chromium both ways. A-37: the high clamp, the low clamp
(`'0000-00-00'`, which the ruling never names), eleven malformed codes at two read sites, the
`'A|'`/`'A'` key ambiguity, the deliberate `'--'`→`null` merge (one row, two counted, both trips,
nothing dropped), purity through both gates, an out-of-domain `today`, and four shape-invalid dates
that must still throw. Constraints: determinism, zero-dep, no DOM in `packages/client`, bare-Node
runnability of the gate, no stray worktrees, the read-only boundary.

**R29-1, at length, because the reasoning is the evidence.** See the status note above for the
full account. The three things that make it a repeat of R28-2 rather than a new class of problem:
the fault reaches **actual persisted bytes**, it is caught by **none** of the four gates, and the
gate that should catch it states in its own ruling that it does. The two controls matter as much
as the fault — the identical mutation in `packages/client/src/ports/memory.ts` is 2 red, and a
lifetime cache in a second store in that same port is 1 red — because they localise the hole to
*the one port no gate executes*, not to the recipe. A-33 residue 2 already names that port as the
uncovered one and sets a trigger (*"a second port-internal defect"*); this is that. The probe the
ruling asks for at 6b-4 now exists (`qa/i7a-idb-rowkeys.mjs`), passes on the shipped tree, and
goes 3 FAIL under the fault, so the cheapest close is to promote it rather than to make 6b-2
cleverer — though binding the capture to the enclosing method's own parameter list would also do
it, and is a smaller diff.

**What I tried on A-32 and could not break.** Three independent oracles (Fliegel–Van Flandern,
Zeller, a brute-force walker), 4.5 million evaluations, nine historical weekday anchors, the
exhaustive round trip over the whole domain, totality on `±Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, the domain
edges in both directions, the roll-over grid against `Date.UTC` for years ≥ 100, `addDays` and
`dateSpan` across the 100 and 1000 boundaries and across a leap year at year 4, the product path
through `PastTripForm` → `createTrip` → the memory port → `fromJSON`, and `validateTrip`'s
density check on a deliberately drifted document. The only two things I found near it are R29-2
(a bound the ruling reasoned about for one branch only) and R29-6 (a residue whose bound is
stated over the wrong noun) — neither is an error in the arithmetic.

**R28-1, at length, because the reasoning is the evidence.**

`derive/summary.ts:23` is `dayNumber(d) = Math.floor(Date.UTC(y, m-1, dd)/86400000)`. `Date.UTC`
carries the ES legacy two-digit-year rule: a `year` argument of 0–99 means 1900–1999. Measured:
`Date.UTC(1,0,1)` is `1901-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`, `Date.UTC(99,0,1)` is `1999-01-01`, and
`Date.UTC(100,0,1)` is `0100-01-01` — so the mangle is exactly the 0–99 window. Consequently
`dayNumber('0001-01-01') === dayNumber('1901-01-01')`, both `-25202`.

`derive/summary.ts:28-30` is the inverse, and it pads the month and the day but not the year:
`` `${dt.getUTCFullYear()}-${p(m)}-${p(d)}` ``. So a genuine year below 1000 comes back with a
short year — `fromDayNumber(dayNumber('0500-06-01'))` is `"500-06-01"` — which `parseIsoDate`,
eight lines above it in the same file, throws `invalid IsoDate` on.

Three consequences, each executed rather than reasoned:

1. **`travelStats` emits a date its own parser rejects.** A row starting `0500-06-01` reports
   `firstVisit: "500-06-01"`. `TravelStatsCountry.firstVisit` is typed `IsoDate`.
2. **Two trips 1900 years apart become one interval.** A year-`0001` trip and a year-`1901` trip
   over the same day-of-year report `daysTravelled: 10`, not 20 — the union collapsed them,
   because they are literally the same day numbers.
3. **The product-reachable one, and it is data loss.** `PastTripForm.tsx:76` gates the Year field
   on `/^\d{4}$/` and nothing else; the input at `:208` does
   `value.replace(/\D/g,'').slice(0,4)`, so a leading zero is preserved and `0202` — a plausible
   mistype of `2020` — is valid. Driven through the real client store over the real memory port,
   exactly as the form does it: `createTrip` accepts the range, `ensureDays` mints 365 days whose
   `date` **and `id`** are `"202-01-01"` … `"202-12-31"`, the document is written to storage, and
   the next cold start gets `TripParseError: expected YYYY-MM-DD (at $.days[0].date)`
   (`serialize/fromJSON.ts:77`). The trip is in storage, it is the only copy, and it can never be
   opened again. `Library.tsx` badges it *"could not be read"* — graceful degradation around data
   that is gone, which is the right UI over the wrong outcome.

   Year `0026` is the quieter half and arguably the worse one, because nothing complains at all:
   the days are minted as `1926-01-01` … `1926-12-31` against a stored `startDate` of
   `0026-01-01`, `validateTrip` returns **0 issues** (its density check runs through the same
   mangled `dayNumber`, so the document is internally consistent in mangled space and only the
   two date *strings* disagree with it), the document round-trips, and `travelStats` reports 365
   days travelled for a trip whose dates are meaningless.

**Why this lands on I-7 rather than only on Phase 1.** `dayNumber`, `fromDayNumber`,
`PastTripForm` and `ensureDays` all predate this increment and the builder did not introduce the
bug. But A-31 Part 4 step 5 justifies the sort-and-sweep with *"an `IsoDate` admits year `0001`,
and a hand-written row would otherwise allocate millions of entries"*, and
`packages/core/test/travelStats.test.ts:280` asserts `daysTravelled === 365` for exactly that row.
That test is green because it is silently measuring **1901**, which also has 365 days. A test that
certifies a wrong answer is worse than no test — it is the artefact the next reader will trust —
and it is I-7's.

**Route: architect first.** Two decisions are needed and neither is a builder's: (1) does `IsoDate`
have a stated lower bound (and does `isIsoDate` / `fromJSON` / `PastTripForm` enforce it), or do
`dayNumber`/`fromDayNumber` get a civil-calendar implementation that does not route through
`Date.UTC`? and (2) A-31's year-`0001` clause is either honoured or withdrawn — it cannot stay as
a justification for an algorithm whose helpers cannot represent the year it names. Then builder,
with `qa/i7-year.mjs` as the acceptance oracle.

**R28-2, and why "the criterion passes" is not the same as "the criterion works".**

A-31 Part 6 did the right thing: it caught that the old grep was *false* (it would have found
`cityCount` and `dayCount`, which have been persisted since Phase 1), withdrew it rather than
reinterpreting it, and replaced it with two mechanical halves. Half (b) is
`test/stats-storage.test.ts:172`:

```js
for (const m of src.matchAll(/([A-Za-z$_][\w$]*)\??\s*:\s*number\b/g)) {
```

That matches a **type declaration**. It cannot match a **value**, and a persisted count is a value.
`bash qa/i7-exit6.sh` runs eight faults, each applied alone in a throwaway `git worktree` at HEAD.
Five are caught. Three are not:

- **F8 — the one that matters.** Both `SUMMARIES.put(summary, id)` call sites in
  `apps/web/src/ports/storage.ts` (`:226`, `:279`) become
  `put({ ...summary, countriesVisited: summary.countryCodes.length, daysTravelled: summary.dayCount }, id)`.
  Those two numbers are now in IndexedDB, on every write, with nothing to recompute them from —
  the literal `countriesVisited: 47` that A-31 Part 6 exists to forbid. Measured under the fault:
  exit criterion 6 **5 pass / 0 fail**; the full suite **795 pass / 0 fail**;
  `tsc -p apps/web/tsconfig.json --noEmit` **clean**, because a spread widens the object type and
  excess-property checking never fires.
- **F6** — the same two counts declared through a one-line `type Tally = number` alias. Green.
- **F4** — `daysAbroad: number` added to `TripSummaryRow` *and minted into every row*. Green in
  **both** halves, because the classifier's `SHAPE` wants a counting suffix and `PLURAL` wants a
  plural domain noun and `daysAbroad` is neither. So half (a)'s stated property — *"a field added
  to the row without being added to the list fails the run"* — is not true for every count-shaped
  field, only for conveniently-named ones.

**KD-64, assessed rather than accepted.** The two entries A-31 Part 6 did not enumerate are both
legitimate and the builder's judgement on them is right: `horizonDays` is a look-ahead duration on
a compile-time `RuleSpec`, never written anywhere, and `TravelStats`' own fields are the return
type of a pure function whose non-persistence is pinned mechanically by the fourth test (which I
verified is live — fault F7 reds it). The hole is not the allow-list. It is the shape of the check.
§0.5 is explicit that *"a rule that cannot catch its own bug does not ship"*, and this rule cannot.
Route: **architect** for what half (b) must actually assert — a check at the value/port level, or
an assertion that the set of keys reaching `SUMMARIES.put` is exactly `TripSummaryRow`'s — and
**builder** for the classifier, which should also cover `packages/tokens/src` (`ROOTS` omits it).

**What I attacked and could not break.**

- **The interval union**, eight ways: `[a,b]` + `[b,c]` sharing an endpoint counts day `b` once
  (20, not 21); adjacency neither invents nor merges a day; a one-day gap stays a gap; a contained
  interval adds nothing; a short interval between two long ones does not truncate the run (32);
  two zero-day trips on the same day are one day; month, year and leap-day rollovers are exact
  (7 / 3 / 2); pre-epoch spans and negative day numbers round-trip.
- **The `today` clamp on its five exact days**: `startDate` → 1, `+1` → 2, `endDate` → full span,
  `endDate+1` → same span via `completed`, `startDate−1` → 0 and `trips.planned: 1`. Two
  simultaneously-active overlapping trips both clamp and union to 10.
- **Purity**, harder than the shipped test: a **deep-frozen** `readonly` input does not throw; two
  calls are deep-equal; the caller's array order is byte-identical afterwards; a shuffled input
  gives a deep-equal result; every output array is fresh (not frozen, so not the input's); and
  mutating the returned `tripIds` does not poison the next call.
- **Grouping**: NFC and NFD `Zürich` are one row; space-, tab-, NBSP- and empty-named cities are
  zero rows, one `unnamedCities` and one `located.cities` each; a city literally named `US|Paris`
  does not collide with `Paris` in `US`, because the country prefix is fixed-width as the comment
  claims. Duplicate `countryCodes` on one row credit the trip once. `tripIds` come out in
  canonical `(startDate, id)` order with no duplicates.
- **A-31 Part 4's closing sentence, through the CLI on three hand-built documents**: a one-city
  trip with nothing placed prints *"nothing could be placed on the map"* with `located.cities 1`;
  a trip with no city at all prints *"no places yet"*; a blank-named city prints *"cities with no
  usable name: 1"*. The two states A-31 says must be distinguishable are distinguishable.
- **The seven injected faults**, re-derived from A-31's wording and re-run: all seven red, blast
  radius measured across the whole suite (M1→4, M2→2, M3→2, M4→2, M5→5, M6→1, M7→1). The
  builder's disclosed near-miss on M7 is genuinely repaired.

**The three "could not verify" items, closed.** (1) The 3→4 rescan against real version-3 rows —
seeded by minting with the shipped `tripSummary` and deleting exactly what I-7 added, then
`refreshLibrary()` + `rescanSummaries()`: every row reaches 4, every census equals a fresh mint,
`saveCount` does not move and `refreshCount` is 3. (2) `travelStats` over a real multi-row library
straight out of storage: `{completed: 2, active: 1}`, `daysTravelled` 28, countries and cities
sorted, the active trip's `lastVisit` clamped, the store's own array untouched. (3) The year-`0001`
case now has a **cost** assertion: 200 rows each spanning `0001-01-01`…`9999-12-31` sweep in
**1.9 ms**, 50,000 rows in **283 ms** — O(n log n) in rows, so a `Set` or a quadratic sweep would
be caught. (That probe is also what first exposed R28-1.)

## Round 27 — I-6a: A-29's stated-country gate and A-30's `refreshSummary` (`master` @ `481b7e8`)

**The verdict first, because this is the round that closes the checkpoint. I-6a is done and it is
sound.** The two-cycle redesign of the summary write path — I-6's `saveIfVersion` rewrite, then
I-6a's `refreshSummary` — ends with a mechanism I could not break: the refresh cannot mint, cannot
create, cannot resurrect, and cannot write a row about a document other than the one its own link
just read. Three MINORs, none of which touches that mechanism.

**The most useful thing this round did was stop reasoning about the IndexedDB port and run it.**
BUILD-NOTES lists it under *"what I could not verify"* — *"asserted by construction and by review
against `saveIfVersion`, which it is a strict subset of"* — with the reason that *"there is no
headless-browser harness in this repo's test suite."* That reason is wrong, and it is wrong in a way
worth naming rather than just correcting: **`qa/browser2.mjs`, `qa/r3-browser.mjs` and
`qa/r4-browser.mjs` have driven real Chromium against real IndexedDB since round 3**, and R4-2 — the
version-token defect that a remembered `epoch` reproduced *"in Chromium, byte for byte"* — is in this
project's own history precisely because someone ran the port instead of reviewing it. The suite has
no browser harness; `qa/` does, and `qa/` is where an unexecuted write path belongs. It is executed
now, two ways, and it is correct. I am not filing that as a finding because the builder disclosed it
rather than hiding it, and because the code turned out to be right; I am recording it because the
next increment that adds a port method should reach for `qa/` rather than for the phrase "asserted by
construction".

**On KD-62, which the builder routed to the architect.** The hole is real and I reproduced it exactly
as disclosed: the thunk mutation typechecks clean, the §4.3 structural grep stays green, and the
entire client suite stays green at 216/216. But two things follow that the disclosure does not have.
First, **there is no live instance** — a static census of `store.ts` finds three `ports.storage`
mutations, each `await`ed inline in the statement that reads for it, and zero named async function
expressions anywhere in the file, so nothing in the codebase walks into this accidentally. Second,
and this is what changes the routing: **the property §4.3 actually claims is an ordering property,
and ordering is observable at the port without any dataflow analysis at all.** *While one chain link
is parked inside a `ports.storage` mutation, no other `ports.storage` mutation may reach the port* —
that is what "the chain serializes writes" means, it is checkable from outside the store by a wrapped
`MemoryStorage` that knows nothing about the store's internals, and it goes red on the thunk mutation
while the grep and the suite do not. `qa/i6a-chain.mjs` is that check, in about twenty lines, and it
is green on the shipped tree. So the choice is not "a weaker-but-checkable property versus a
stronger-but-unimplementable one"; the stronger property is implementable, and the grep was always
the approximation rather than the claim. **That makes it R27-2, a builder item, not an architect
ruling.**

### What I attacked and could **not** break

- **A-29's gate, exhaustively.** All 2,704 two-ASCII-letter strings driven through `tripSummary`
  and compared against a regex-free formulation of Part 3: zero disagreements. 36 whitespace,
  length and control-character shapes: zero. A 15-case Unicode battery — Cyrillic `НР`/`АТ`, Greek
  `ΕΗ` (whose ASCII twin *is* an index code), fullwidth `ＨＲ`, combining marks, the `🇦🇹`
  regional-indicator pair, `ﬀ`, `ı`, `ſ`, `İ`, `KK` — every one refused. **The step order is
  pinned**: `'ıl'`, `'ſe'`, `'ıe'` and `'gı'` all uppercase to real index codes and are all refused
  because the regex runs first, and no ASCII-letter pair can uppercase to anything but two ASCII
  capitals, so step 3 can never widen step 2. Every index code is itself `/^[A-Z]{2}$/`, so the
  membership set cannot be case-fooled either.
- **Per-city isolation and non-additivity.** Three cities, only the middle one unattributable, the
  other two stating a wrong `JP`: each city gets its own answer, `JP` never reaches `countryCodes`,
  the union is `AT,CZ,HR` sorted, and all of it is stable under re-ordering the cities. Over 1,244
  (code × coordinate) pairs, `countrySource` is `null` exactly when `countryCode` is, the code
  always matches `/^[A-Z]{2}$/`, and a non-null coordinate always wins.
- **The fence, five ways.** Two tabs with A open and idle *and never having written* (the version
  that does not pass for the wrong reason); two tabs rescanning the same rows concurrently; the CAS
  racing a `deleteTrip` on the same document across two stores; the CAS racing a document save in
  both orders; and the same two races again in **real IndexedDB**. In every one: no fence moved for
  a summary write, no document was written, no deleted trip came back, and every row carried its own
  countries. `delete`, `saveIfVersion` and `refreshSummary` are each one `readwrite` transaction over
  the same three object stores, so IndexedDB serializes them and there is no interleaving point.
- **The IndexedDB port against the memory port, differentially.** A 14-call script — create,
  refresh, refresh again, refresh an absent id, refresh with a wrong expectation, move the fence
  underneath, refresh stale, refresh current, delete, refresh deleted, recreate, refresh — run
  against both ports. **Identical, outcome by outcome, field by field.** Both half-deleted shapes
  (envelope without document, document without envelope) are refused by both, which is A-30 (c)'s
  check doing the job the builder built it for and could not test.
- **Degradation.** A `refreshSummary` that *rejects* mid-pass surfaces to the caller, clears
  `rescan.running` in the `finally`, reports `'stale'` rather than `'complete'`, is **not** mis-filed
  as an unreadable document, does not poison the chain (a later pass completes and every row
  converges), and writes no document at any point.
- **The orphan row's remaining sharp edge, and why it is not a finding.** A summary row whose
  document is gone stays in the library forever, and clicking its card raises the raw internal
  `openTrip: no trip t-orphan in storage`. It is not filed because it is **unreachable through the
  shipped IndexedDB port**: `delete` and `saveIfVersion` are each single atomic transactions over all
  three object stores, and `ensureReady()` stamps any document that lacks an envelope, so no code
  path can produce the shape. R26-3's fix is correctly defensive rather than load-bearing. Deleting
  the card cleans it up, verified.
- **The census assertion's other blind spot, checked rather than assumed.** `ports.storage` is
  reached from `store.ts` and nowhere else in `packages/client/src`, `apps/web/src` never touches a
  port method directly, and there is no aliasing anywhere — so the literal-text census is accurate
  today even though it would not catch an alias. Recorded inside R27-2 rather than separately.

## Round 26 — I-6: the widened `TripSummaryRow` and the `SUMMARY_VERSION` rescan (`master` @ `0f52c4c`)

ROADMAP calls I-6 *"the riskiest increment in the phase"*, and the risk it names — a summary is a
copy, so §0.6 governs it — is not where the defects are. **The write path is sound.** The
bookkeeping around it is where four of the six findings live, and all four have the same shape:
a fact about *the last pass* outliving the thing it was a fact about.

**The load-bearing question first, because it deserves a plain answer. KD-57 is correct, and the
builder undersold it.** The claim is that reusing `writeAndSettle` for a non-active document would
violate §2.2a A-7. I did not take that on trust; I built it. In a throwaway worktree the rescan's
non-active branch becomes `await writeAndSettle(doc, doc, null, stored.version)` — four lines, and
**it compiles clean**, which is the first thing worth knowing: nothing in the type system can see
this. A-7's guard reads

```ts
if (!stillOurs && toWrite !== startedFrom) { /* refuse: no install, no fence, no re-arm */ }
```

and for a self-contained rewrite of trip **Y** while trip **X** is active, `stillOurs` is false but
`toWrite === startedFrom` — both are Y — so the guard does not fire and execution falls into the
ordinary `set`. Measured, with X active at storage version `1.4`:

| after the rescan of trip Y | shipped (`attemptSave` route) | KD-57's refused option |
|---|---|---|
| `persistence.savedVersion` | `1.4` — X's own | **`1.5` — minted for Y** |
| `persistence.savedDoc` | X's document | **Y's document** |
| `dirty()` with nothing typed | false | **true** |
| the user's next keystroke + flush | `'idle'`, edit in storage | **`'conflict'`, edit stranded in memory** |
| *Merge and save*, the only offered escape | converges | **throws** `mergeTrips: base, local and remote must be the same trip (got t-hr, t-at, t-at)` |

That last row is the consequence KD-57 does not state and it is the sharpest one. §2.2a's Merge row
and A-7's own argument both make `savedDoc` the three-way ancestor; a fence pointing at another
trip therefore does not merely mis-refuse a write, it makes the button offered to resolve the
refusal *unreachable*. A user in that state has a conflict banner, a Merge button that throws, and
an edit only in memory. The builder's route never enters that state, and not by luck:
`attemptSave` reads `state.doc` itself and returns early unless `forTripId` matches it
(`store.ts:404-407`), so it is structurally incapable of being aimed at a non-active document, and
`runRescan` calls it only under `if (state.doc && state.doc.id === id)` with no `await` between
the test and the call. **The fix did not move the bug; the two paths are disjoint by
construction.** Two shipped tests go red under the mutation — the builder's own fence test and the
§4.3 structural grep — so this is pinned rather than merely argued.

**What I could not break, listed so "sound" is a conclusion and not an absence of effort.** The
active trip's identity changing mid-pass (`openTrip` landing between two rows); `closeTrip` on the
very document being rescanned; three `rescanSummaries()` calls joining one pass with an edit
dispatched under it; a delete arriving straight at the port between the rescan's `load` and its
`saveIfVersion`; 40 rows in two countries. In every one of them every row was computed from its own
document, no row carried another row's countries, `activeTripId` never moved, `state.doc` was never
a non-active document, the undo stack was neither cleared nor grown, the retirement ledger never
crossed a trip, and the fence ended on the active trip's own stored version.

### Findings

| id | sev | where | defect | repro | routing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **R26-1** | **MAJOR** | `packages/client/src/store/store.ts:806-807` | Every pass ends `const library = await ports.storage.listTrips(); set({ ...state, library, … })` **outside** any `chainOntoSaving` callback. §4.3 exempts `listTrips` from the chain because it is a *read* — but the `set` that consumes it is a **write to `state.library`** that replaces the whole array with a snapshot taken at an earlier moment, and `deleteTrip` removes a row from `state.library` inside a chain link (`:1143-1150`) that this read is not ordered against. Park the pass's `listTrips()`, delete a trip while it is parked, release: **the deleted trip's card is back in the library the user is looking at**, `summaryScan` reports `complete`, and clicking it raises the raw internal `openTrip: no trip doomed in storage`. ### What I attacked and could **not** break

- **The KD-57 counterfactual, both directions.** Not just "does the shipped path avoid it" but
  "does the refused path actually fail" — it does, five ways (table above), and the failure is
  invisible to `tsc`. `bash qa/i6-fence.sh`.
- **The §4.3 ceiling, three mutations.** M1 the bare async IIFE (the builder's own claim,
  re-derived), M2 a third off-chain call site, M3 the same write hoisted one frame out of the
  callback while staying ordered. All three red. `bash qa/i6-ceiling.sh`.
- **The "closed list of six" claim, count *and* substance.** `retirement-ledger.test.ts` is
  byte-identical since `4eabf08`, still finds exactly the six methods, and `reseed: true` still
  occurs exactly 7 times. Substantively: over a full pass with a trip open, `runRescan` emitted 7
  state updates and **0** of them moved `doc` or `activeTripId`; the only `persistence` movement
  was the active trip's own `attemptSave`; `set` takes its step-1 identity branch on every rescan
  update because `next.doc === state.doc`, so the ledger's absorb/re-assert path is never entered.
- **Cross-contamination, six ways.** Three trips in three countries under: a mid-pass `openTrip`,
  a mid-pass `closeTrip`, three joined `rescanSummaries()` calls with an edit dispatched under
  them, a port-level delete between `load` and `saveIfVersion`, a transient third-writer refusal,
  and 40 rows alternating `AT`/`HR`. Every row carried its own countries and matched its own
  document's `id` and `title`. `qa/i6-race.mjs`, `qa/i6-converge.mjs`.
- **Resurrection in storage.** `saveIfVersion` with a non-null expectation against an absent
  record is refused (`memory.ts:98` — `matches = exists ? … : expectedVersion === null`), so the
  rescan cannot write back a trip a second tab destroyed under it. R26-1 is the *in-memory row*,
  not the document.
- **Degradation under a failing port.** `storage.failAll` mid-pass: `rescan.running` is cleared by
  the `finally`, `summaryScan` reports `'stale'` rather than `'complete'`, the failure surfaces to
  the caller (and `App.tsx:37-39` catches it into the error banner) rather than being swallowed, it
  is **not** mis-filed as an unreadable document, and the `chainOntoSaving` queue is not poisoned —
  a later pass completes normally. `qa/i6-race.mjs` §H.
- **`tripSummary`'s `null` handling, which is `countryOf`'s first real consumer.** A mid-Atlantic
  city centre carries `null` into `cities[].countryCode` and is *excluded* from `countryCodes` —
  never `null`, never `undefined`, never the string `"null"`, never snapped to a neighbour. A
  wholly unattributable trip is `[]`. Out-of-range and `NaN` coordinates do not crash. A stop with
  `place: {kind:'none'}` is counted as a stop and contributes no country. Zero cities, zero days.
  `qa/i6-summary.mjs`.
- **Purity and determinism of the widened row.** Two calls byte-identical; the trip is not mutated;
  the index is not mutated; `countryCodes` sorted; `cities` in display order, not sort order.
- **The active document's in-flight edit.** The rescan does write it early — `attemptSave` has no
  `dirty()` skip — so a half-typed title reaches storage ahead of the 400 ms debounce. Recorded
  rather than filed: it is the same write the debounce would have made 400 ms later, the store is
  left `'idle'` with `savedDoc === doc`, and nothing is lost. Worth knowing only because a method
  named for a summary refresh is also a document write. `qa/i6-race.mjs` §F.
- **`summaryScan`'s completeness claim.** `'recomputing'` wins over `'complete'` while a pass runs;
  a row carrying a *higher* `summaryVersion` than this build's is treated as current rather than
  rescanned; an absent field reads as below every version. The only way I got it to lie is R26-2,
  and it lies in the safe direction.

### Why this is not a BLOCKER round

Every finding here is recoverable and none of them crosses a trip boundary. R26-1 is the closest
call and I considered MAJOR carefully against BLOCKER: it puts a card on screen for a trip that no
longer exists, which is a delete visibly not working — but storage is correct at every instant, no
document is resurrected, no other trip's data is shown, and the next boot's `refreshLibrary()`
removes it. The thing that would have made I-6 a blocker round is a summary computed from the wrong
document or a fence moved to the wrong trip, and I went at both hard: the first across six
concurrency shapes and 40 rows, the second by building the failure KD-57 refuses and confirming the
shipped path cannot reach it. **The mechanism is sound. The bookkeeping around it has four bugs and
they are all the same bug — an observation about the last pass outliving the thing it observed —
which is worth saying to the builder as one sentence rather than four.**

## Round 25 — the I-5 closure round (`master` @ `32efd1e`)

Fifth pass on the country index, and a confirmation pass rather than a hunt: the builder had just
closed R24-2, R24-3 and R24-4 plus four stale sites the architect found while fixing R24-1. **The
fix holds under attack, including four ways of breaking it nobody had tried, and the one item the
builder left explicitly unresolved is now resolved and was never a bug.** Four MINORs, and one of
them is the finding the builder itself asked to have routed.

The one thing worth reading twice: **`qa/i5b-mutants.sh`'s "five stale rows" have not been stale
since `99c2e84`.** Round 24 repaired them, said so in its own status note, and BUILD-NOTES has now
carried the superseded disclosure through two consecutive addenda — a stale claim propagating
because each pass copied the previous pass's caveat instead of running the script. Running it takes
14 seconds and every one of its 26 mutations applies. That is the same failure mode as R24-2 and
R24-4, one level up: a *caveat* that reads as a result.
